content: In botanical terms, a rhizome is a horizontal stem of a plant that typically grows underground. It often produces roots and shoots from its nodes. Examples of plants with underground rhizomes include ginger, hops, and turmeric, which are notable for their medicinal properties. Additionally, certain weeds such as Johnson grass, Bermuda grass, and purple nut sedge also possess rhizomes. Some plants, however, have rhizomes that grow above ground or rest at the soil surface. Examples include certain species of Iris and ferns, where the spreading stems are classified as rhizomes. Rhizomes are also referred to as creeping rootstalks or rootstocks. It is important to distinguish rhizomes from stolons. While both are horizontal stems, a rhizome serves as the main stem of the plant, whereas a stolon originates from an existing stem. Stolons typically have long internodes and produce new shoots at their ends, as seen in strawberry plants. In contrast, rhizomes generally have short internodes, with roots emerging from the lower side of the nodes and new upward-growing shoots developing from the upper side. Gardeners often utilize rhizomes for plant propagation through a method known as vegetative reproduction. Plants commonly propagated in this manner include asparagus, ginger, irises, Lily of the Valley, Cannas, and sympodial orchids. A stem tuber is a thickened portion of a rhizome or stolon that has been modified to function as a storage organ. These tubers are typically rich in starch. For instance, the common potato is a modified stolon and serves as a classic example of a tuber. However, the term tuber is sometimes used inaccurately and may be applied to plants with rhizomes. In addition to its botanical significance, the concept of the rhizome has been employed metaphorically in the philosophy of Gilles Deleuze and Félix Guattari.
